claim: SEL-5 is the C. elegans orthologue of mammalian AP2-associated kinase AAK1.
source: In this study, we show that SEL-5, the C. elegans orthologue of mammalian AP2-associated kinase AAK1, acts together with the retromer complex as a positive regulator of EGL-20/Wnt signalling during the migration of QL neuroblast daughter cells.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction, establishing the relationship between SEL-5 and AAK1.

claim: SEL-5 acts together with the retromer complex as a positive regulator of EGL-20/Wnt signalling during the migration of QL neuroblast daughter cells.
source: In this study, we show that SEL-5, the C. elegans orthologue of mammalian AP2-associated kinase AAK1, acts together with the retromer complex as a positive regulator of EGL-20/Wnt signalling during the migration of QL neuroblast daughter cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: SEL-5 kinase activity is not required for its role in neuronal migration.
source: Importantly, SEL-5 kinase activity is not required for its role in neuronal migration or excretory cell outgrowth, and neither of these processes is dependent on DPY-23/AP2M1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments with kinase-dead SEL-5 mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: SEL-5 kinase activity is not required for its role in excretory cell outgrowth.
source: Importantly, SEL-5 kinase activity is not required for its role in neuronal migration or excretory cell outgrowth, and neither of these processes is dependent on DPY-23/AP2M1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments with kinase-dead SEL-5 mutants shown in Figure 6G.

claim: DPY-23/AP2M1 phosphorylation is not required for neuronal migration.
source: Importantly, SEL-5 kinase activity is not required for its role in neuronal migration or excretory cell outgrowth, and neither of these processes is dependent on DPY-23/AP2M1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with dpy-23(mew25) mutants shown in Figure 5D.

claim: DPY-23/AP2M1 phosphorylation is not required for excretory cell outgrowth.
source: Importantly, SEL-5 kinase activity is not required for its role in neuronal migration or excretory cell outgrowth, and neither of these processes is dependent on DPY-23/AP2M1 phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experiments with dpy-23(mew25) mutants shown in Figure 6H.

claim: RNAi against sel-5 significantly increased the QL.d migration defect of vps-29(tm1320).
source: RNAi against sel-5 significantly increased the QL.d migration defect of vps-29(tm1320) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly shown in the RNAi experiments presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Mutation of sel-5 alone did not affect QL.d migration.
source: Similarly to RNAi results, mutation of sel-5 alone did not affect QL.d migration while sel-5 vps-29 double mutants displayed an almost fully penetrant defect (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: sel-5 vps-29 double mutants displayed an almost fully penetrant QL.d migration defect.
source: Similarly to RNAi results, mutation of sel-5 alone did not affect QL.d migration while sel-5 vps-29 double mutants displayed an almost fully penetrant defect (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: The loss of vps-29 affects EGL-20/Wnt signalling at the level of Wnt production.
source: The loss of vps-29 affects EGL-20/Wnt signalling at the level of Wnt production (Yang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from a previous publication.

claim: The loss of sel-5 strongly increased the weak QL.d migration defect of the lin-17/Frizzled mutants.
source: The loss of sel-5 strongly increased the weak QL.d migration defect of the lin-17/Frizzled mutants but did not affect the already more penetrant QL.d defect of mig-1/Frizzled mutant animals (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: The loss of sel-5 did not affect the QL.d defect of mig-1/Frizzled mutant animals.
source: The loss of sel-5 strongly increased the weak QL.d migration defect of the lin-17/Frizzled mutants but did not affect the already more penetrant QL.d defect of mig-1/Frizzled mutant animals (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 1D.

claim: Weakly penetrant ALM polarization defects were observed in both sel-5(ok363) vps-29 and sel-5(ok149) vps-29 double mutants.
source: We observed weakly penetrant ALM polarization defects in both sel-5(ok363) vps-29 and sel-5(ok149) vps-29 double mutants, a very mild PLM polarization defect was detected in a strain carrying the ok149 allele (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Table 1.

claim: A very mild PLM polarization defect was detected in sel-5(ok149) vps-29 mutants.
source: We observed weakly penetrant ALM polarization defects in both sel-5(ok363) vps-29 and sel-5(ok149) vps-29 double mutants, a very mild PLM polarization defect was detected in a strain carrying the ok149 allele (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Table 1.

claim: Mildly penetrant anterior displacement of the CAN neuron was observed in sel-5 vps-29 double mutants.
source: In addition, mildly penetrant anterior displacement of the CAN neuron was observed in the double mutants, while approximately 17% of the double mutant animals carrying the ok149 allele did not correctly form the phasmid sensillum, which indicates defects in T cell polarization (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Table 1.

claim: Approximately 17% of sel-5(ok149) vps-29 double mutant animals did not correctly form the phasmid sensillum.
source: In addition, mildly penetrant anterior displacement of the CAN neuron was observed in the double mutants, while approximately 17% of the double mutant animals carrying the ok149 allele did not correctly form the phasmid sensillum, which indicates defects in T cell polarization (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Table 1.

claim: Reduced brood size was observed in sel-5 vps-29 double mutants compared to controls.
source: Apart from these Wnt-dependent phenotypes, we also observed reduced brood size in the double mutants compared to controls (Table 1), defective tail formation (Figure 1E), and a progressive egg-laying defect leading to a bag-of-worms phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in the data presented in Table 1.

claim: Defective tail formation was observed in sel-5 vps-29 double mutants.
source: Apart from these Wnt-dependent phenotypes, we also observed reduced brood size in the double mutants compared to controls (Table 1), defective tail formation (Figure 1E), and a progressive egg-laying defect leading to a bag-of-worms phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: A progressive egg-laying defect leading to a bag-of-worms phenotype was observed in sel-5 vps-29 double mutants.
source: Apart from these Wnt-dependent phenotypes, we also observed reduced brood size in the double mutants compared to controls (Table 1), defective tail formation (Figure 1E), and a progressive egg-laying defect leading to a bag-of-worms phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the results.

claim: Shorter than wild type transcripts were amplified from both sel-5(ok363) and sel-5(ok149) animals.
source: We were able to amplify shorter than wild type transcripts from both sel-5(ok363) and sel-5(ok149) animals using primers in exon 1 and exon 17 (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The ok363 transcript can give rise to a protein containing amino acids 1–243 of the wild type protein followed by additional 32 amino acids.
source: Sequencing of the ok363 transcript revealed that amino acids 1–243 of the wild type protein followed by additional 32 amino acids would be translated due to a frameshift and a premature stop codon.
evidence: This is based on sequencing data of the transcript.

claim: The ok149 transcript can give rise to a protein containing the first 153 amino acids of SEL-5 followed by 21 additional amino acids and is devoid of the active site.
source: In agreement with data published by Fares and Greenwald, 1999, sequencing of the ok149 transcript revealed that it can give rise to a protein containing the first 153 amino acids of SEL-5 followed by 21 additional amino acids and thus is devoid of the active site (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is based on sequencing data of the transcript and comparison with published data.

claim: The expression of SEL-5 from the egl-20 promoter resulted in a significant rescue of the QL.d migration defect of sel-5 vps-29 double mutants.
source: The expression of SEL-5 from the egl-20 promoter (Coudreuse et al., 2006) resulted in a significant rescue of the QL.d migration defect of sel-5 vps-29 double mutants albeit not to the level of vps-29 single mutants (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 2A.

claim: No rescue was obtained when SEL-5 was expressed from the wrt-2 promoter.
source: No rescue was obtained when SEL-5 was expressed from the wrt-2 promoter that is active in the seam cells and the Q cells (Aspöck et al., 1999; Middelkoop et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a result of the rescue experiments.

claim: sel-5 is required in the EGL-20/Wnt-producing cells to control QL.d migration.
source: These data suggest that sel-5 is required in the EGL-20/Wnt-producing cells to control QL.d migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: A similar level of rescue as with egl-20 promoter was obtained when SEL-5 was expressed from hlh-1 promoter specific for the body wall muscle cells.
source: However, a similar level of rescue as with egl-20 promoter was obtained also when SEL-5 was expressed from hlh-1 promoter specific for the body wall muscle cells (Krause et al., 1990; Harfe et al., 1998).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 2A.

claim: When SEL-5 was simultaneously expressed from the egl-20 and hlh-1 promoters, the rescue almost reached the background frequency of the QL.d defect caused by vps-29 alone.
source: When SEL-5 was simultaneously expressed from the egl-20 and hlh-1 promoters, the rescue almost reached the background frequency of the QL.d defect, caused by vps-29 alone (Figures 1D and 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 2A.

claim: sel-5 is expressed broadly, but at a low level.
source: Microscopic analyses of both strains revealed that sel-5 is expressed broadly, but at a low level judged by the intensity of the GFP signal.
evidence: This is based on microscopic analysis of GFP reporter strains.

claim: The most prominent sel-5 expression was observed in the gonad from the beginning of its development.
source: The most prominent expression was observed in the gonad from the beginning of its development (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: sel-5 expression was observed in the developing oocytes, in the vulva, in epidermal cells, and in the rectal epithelial cells.
source: Expression was further observed in the developing oocytes, in the vulva, in epidermal cells, and most notably, in the rectal epithelial cells that are known to produce EGL-20/Wnt (Whangbo and Kenyon, 1999; Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: GFP::SEL-5 fusion protein localized to punctate structures located close to the cell surface in oocytes and epidermal seam cells.
source: Interestingly, oocytes and epidermal seam cells expressing the GFP::SEL-5 fusion protein revealed its distinct subcellular localization. Protein localized to punctate structures located close to the cell surface (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The subcellular distribution pattern of SEL-5 resembles the subcellular distribution of human AAK1.
source: This pattern resembles the subcellular distribution of human AAK1 (Conner and Schmid, 2002), hinting that SEL-5 could be involved in regulating intracellular transport similar to AAK1.
evidence: This is based on comparison with published data on AAK1 localization.

claim: The level of phosphorylated endogenous DPY-23 at T160 is reduced in sel-5 mutants compared to wild type animals.
source: A phospho-specific antibody recognizing phosphorylated threonine T160 (T156 in mammalian AP2M1) of DPY-23 (Hollopeter et al., 2014) revealed a decrease in the level of phosphorylated endogenous DPY-23 in sel-5 mutants compared to wild type animals (Figure 3A, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot analysis in Figure 3A.

claim: T160 phosphorylation was reduced on overexpressed GFP-tagged DPY-23 in sel-5 mutants.
source: Similarly, T160 phosphorylation was reduced on overexpressed GFP-tagged DPY-23 (Figure 3B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot analysis in Figure 3B.

claim: The levels of MIG-14::GFP did not change significantly in sel-5 vps-29 compared to the vps-29 single mutant.
source: However, the levels of MIG-14::GFP did not change significantly in sel-5 vps-29 compared to the vps-29 single mutant (Figure 3C and D, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot analysis in Figure 3D.

claim: MIG-14::GFP did not re-localize to the plasma membrane in sel-5 or sel-5 vps-29 mutants.
source: Importantly, MIG-14::GFP did not re-localize to the plasma membrane in sel-5 or sel-5 vps-29 mutants, in striking contrast to the MIG-14::GFP behaviour in animals treated with dpy-23 RNAi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The significant increase in QL.d migration defects in sel-5 vps-29 compared to vps-29 cannot be attributed to changes in MIG-14/Wls levels.
source: We therefore concluded that the significant increase in QL.d migration defects in sel-5 vps-29 compared to vps-29 cannot be attributed to changes in MIG-14/Wls levels.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the MIG-14::GFP level measurements.

claim: The Wnt-related phenotypes in sel-5 vps-29 mutants do not arise from a defect in MIG-14 internalization.
source: This excludes the possibility that the Wnt-related phenotypes in sel-5 vps-29 mutants arise from a defect in MIG-14 internalization.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that MIG-14::GFP does not relocalize to the plasma membrane.

claim: The number of EGL-20 puncta in sel-5 mutants was not significantly different from that in control animals.
source: While the number of EGL-20 puncta in sel-5 mutants was not significantly different from that in control animals, in sel-5 vps-29 mutants the number of puncta was substantially reduced.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: In sel-5 vps-29 mutants the number of EGL-20 puncta was substantially reduced.
source: While the number of EGL-20 puncta in sel-5 mutants was not significantly different from that in control animals, in sel-5 vps-29 mutants the number of puncta was substantially reduced.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4C.

claim: The EGL-20 gradient was shorter in vps-29 sel-5 double mutants than in wild type controls.
source: While EGL-20 gradient formation in neither sel-5 nor vps-29 was significantly affected, the EGL-20 gradient was shorter in vps-29 sel-5 double mutants than in wild type controls (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 4E.

claim: sel-5 plays a subtle role in EGL-20 gradient formation.
source: Our data thus support the notion that sel-5 plays a subtle role in EGL-20 gradient formation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EGL-20 gradient analysis.

claim: Mutant SEL-5 proteins carrying K75A or D178A point mutations could rescue the QL migration phenotype when expressed under the control of the egl-20 promoter.
source: When expressed under the control of the egl-20 promoter, the mutant SEL-5 proteins could still rescue the QL migration phenotype (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 5A.

claim: SEL-5 kinase activity is not responsible for the phenotypes observed in sel-5 vps-29 mutants.
source: This indicates that SEL-5 kinase activity is not responsible for the phenotypes observed in sel-5 vps-29 mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments with kinase-dead SEL-5 mutants.

claim: Homozygous dpy-23(mew25) mutants are viable and look superficially wild type.
source: Characterization of dpy-23(mew25) animals revealed that homozygous mutants are viable; they are not dumpy and look superficially wild type.
evidence: This is based on phenotypic characterization of the mutant.

claim: No DPY-23 phosphorylation was detected in dpy-23(mew25) animals.
source: This indicates that the mutants do not suffer from a gross endocytosis defect, even though no DPY-23 phosphorylation was detected in dpy-23(mew25) animals (Figure 5B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is shown in the Western blot analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: dpy-23(mew25) is able to rescue the 'jowls' phenotype of fcho-1(ox477) mutants.
source: In compliance with previous findings using dpy-23 alleles that harbour mutations changing the T160 amino acid (Hollopeter et al., 2014; Partlow et al., 2019), mew25 is able to rescue the 'jowls' phenotype of fcho-1(ox477) mutants (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Animals carrying dpy-23(mew25) alone or in combination with sel-5(ok149) did not show any defects in QL.d migration.
source: We then asked whether complete loss of DPY-23 phosphorylation would lead to a QL.d migration defect. Animals carrying dpy-23(mew25) alone or in combination with sel-5(ok149) did not show any defects in QL.d migration (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 5D.

claim: MIG-14::GFP did not re-localize to the plasma membrane in dpy-23(mew25).
source: Furthermore, MIG-14::GFP did not re-localize to the plasma membrane in dpy-23(mew25) similar to the sel-5 mutants and unlike in dpy-23 RNAi animals (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The role of SEL-5 in the regulation of QL.d migration is not dependent on its kinase activity.
source: Together, these observations strongly suggest that the role of SEL-5 in the regulation of QL.d migration is not dependent on its kinase activity and, moreover, that DPY-23 phosphorylation at T160 is not a major regulatory event in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments and dpy-23(mew25) analysis.

claim: DPY-23 phosphorylation at T160 is not a major regulatory event in QL.d migration.
source: Together, these observations strongly suggest that the role of SEL-5 in the regulation of QL.d migration is not dependent on its kinase activity and, moreover, that DPY-23 phosphorylation at T160 is not a major regulatory event in this process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the rescue experiments and dpy-23(mew25) analysis.

claim: In more than 60% of the sel-5 vps-29 mutants the posterior canals stopped at various positions anterior to the rectum.
source: While the posterior canal length in sel-5 or vps-29 single mutants was indistinguishable from the wild type controls, in more than 60% of the sel-5 vps-29 mutants the posterior canals stopped at various positions anterior to the rectum (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6B.

claim: The posterior canal on the right side of the animal was significantly more affected than its counterpart on the left side in sel-5(ok149) vps-29 double mutants.
source: Interestingly, the posterior canal on the right side of the animal was significantly more affected than its counterpart on the left side in sel-5 vps-29 double mutants carrying the ok149 allele (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6D.

claim: In sel-5 vps-29 mutants the posterior canals of the excretory cell are shorter already at the time of hatching.
source: Comparison of canal lengths at several time points within a 24 hr interval after hatching revealed that in sel-5 vps-29 double mutants the posterior canals of the excretory cell are shorter already at the time of hatching and the growth defect prevails throughout larval development (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6E.

claim: The growth defect of posterior canals prevails throughout larval development in sel-5 vps-29 mutants.
source: Comparison of canal lengths at several time points within a 24 hr interval after hatching revealed that in sel-5 vps-29 double mutants the posterior canals of the excretory cell are shorter already at the time of hatching and the growth defect prevails throughout larval development (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6E.

claim: Significant shortening of posterior canals was observed with RNAi against vps-35, vps-26, and snx-3 in sel-5(ok149) background.
source: We performed RNAi against vps-35, vps-26, snx-1, and snx-3 in sel-5(ok149) background and assessed posterior canal length. Except for snx-1 RNAi, significant shortening was observed with RNAi against all other retromer subunits, with vps-35 showing the strongest phenotype (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6F.

claim: The whole retromer complex acts together with sel-5 to control excretory canal outgrowth.
source: These data confirm that the whole retromer complex acts together with sel-5 to control excretory canal outgrowth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the RNAi experiments against retromer subunits.

claim: The expression of SEL-5 from the pgp-12 promoter almost fully rescued the excretory cell shortening.
source: As shown in Figure 6G, the expression of SEL-5 from the pgp-12 promoter almost fully rescued the excretory cell shortening while the expression of SEL-5 from the muscle-specific hlh-1 promoter did not affect the excretory cell phenotype of the sel-5 vps-29 double mutants.
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 6G.

claim: The expression of SEL-5 from the muscle-specific hlh-1 promoter did not affect the excretory cell phenotype of the sel-5 vps-29 double mutants.
source: As shown in Figure 6G, the expression of SEL-5 from the pgp-12 promoter almost fully rescued the excretory cell shortening while the expression of SEL-5 from the muscle-specific hlh-1 promoter did not affect the excretory cell phenotype of the sel-5 vps-29 double mutants.
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 6G.

claim: The excretory canal length was efficiently rescued by the SEL-5D178A variant expressed from pgp-12 promoter.
source: As in the case of the QL.d migration defect, the excretory canal length was efficiently rescued also by the SEL-5D178A variant expressed from pgp-12 promoter arguing that SEL-5 kinase activity is not required for canal extension (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 6G.

claim: Expression of VPS-29 in the excretory cell partially rescued canal shortening.
source: Expression of VPS-29 in the excretory cell partially rescued canal shortening, suggesting that SEL-5 and the retromer complex act together within the same cell to regulate canal length.
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 6G.

claim: SEL-5 and the retromer complex act together within the same cell to regulate canal length.
source: Expression of VPS-29 in the excretory cell partially rescued canal shortening, suggesting that SEL-5 and the retromer complex act together within the same cell to regulate canal length.
evidence: This is inferred from the VPS-29 rescue experiment.

claim: The expression of SEL-5 from the col-10 promoter resulted in a significant rescue of the excretory canal shortening.
source: Interestingly, the expression of SEL-5 from the col-10 promoter, which is active in the hypodermis (Spencer et al., 2001), also resulted in a significant rescue of the excretory canal shortening.
evidence: This is shown in the rescue experiments in Figure 6G.

claim: SEL-5 activity in both the excretory cell and the hypodermis contributes to the regulation of canal outgrowth.
source: This suggests that SEL-5 activity in both the excretory cell and the hypodermis contributes to the regulation of canal outgrowth.
evidence: This is inferred from the tissue-specific rescue experiments.

claim: No canal shortening was observed in animals carrying dpy-23(mew25) alone.
source: No canal shortening was observed in animals carrying dpy-23(mew25) alone (Figure 6H), while only very mild shortening was occasionally observed in either sel-5; dpy-23(mew25) or vps-29; dpy-23(mew25).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 6H.

claim: The role of SEL-5 in excretory canal outgrowth is not dependent on DPY-23 phosphorylation at T160.
source: These observations are consistent with a role of SEL-5 in excretory canal outgrowth that is not dependent on DPY-23 phosphorylation at T160.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dpy-23(mew25) analysis.

claim: lin-17/Frizzled mutants show an overgrowth of the posterior excretory cell canals past the rectum into the tip of the tail.
source: lin-17/Frizzled mutants have been reported to show an overgrowth of the posterior excretory cell canals past the rectum into the tip of the tail (Hedgecock et al., 1987)
evidence: This is cited from a previous publication.

claim: Loss of axl-1 resulted in ectopic branching of the posterior excretory canal without affecting canal length.
source: while loss of axl-1, one of the two C. elegans Axin orthologues, resulted in ectopic branching of the posterior excretory canal without affecting canal length.
evidence: This is cited from a previous publication.

claim: Ectopic branching in axl-1 mutants could be rescued by simultaneous loss of bar-1/β-catenin or pop-1/Tcf expression.
source: Ectopic branching in axl-1 mutants could be rescued by simultaneous loss of bar-1/β-catenin or pop-1/Tcf expression (Oosterveen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from a previous publication.

claim: Among the four Wnts tested (EGL-20, LIN-44, CWN-1, CWN-2), only mutants in lin-44/Wnt exhibited an almost fully penetrant posterior excretory canal overgrowth phenotype.
source: Among the four Wnts tested (EGL-20, LIN-44, CWN-1, CWN-2), only mutants in lin-44/Wnt exhibited an almost fully penetrant posterior excretory canal overgrowth phenotype, as observed in lin-17/Frizzled mutants (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: Mild canal shortening was observed in cwn-2/Wnt and cfz-2/Frizzled mutants.
source: Mild canal shortening was observed in cwn-2/Wnt and cfz-2/Frizzled mutants, while a very weak overgrowth phenotype could be detected in egl-20/Wnt mutants (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: A very weak overgrowth phenotype could be detected in egl-20/Wnt mutants.
source: Mild canal shortening was observed in cwn-2/Wnt and cfz-2/Frizzled mutants, while a very weak overgrowth phenotype could be detected in egl-20/Wnt mutants (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: No change in excretory canal length was displayed by cwn-1/Wnt or mig-1/Frizzled mutants.
source: No change in excretory canal length was displayed by cwn-1/Wnt or mig-1/Frizzled mutants.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: Highly penetrant canal overgrowth was observed in mig-14/Wls mutants.
source: Interestingly, highly penetrant canal overgrowth was also observed in mig-14/Wls mutants, while loss of mig-5/Dishevelled or dsh-1/Dishevelled resulted in a partially penetrant overgrowth phenotype (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: Loss of mig-5/Dishevelled or dsh-1/Dishevelled resulted in a partially penetrant overgrowth phenotype.
source: Interestingly, highly penetrant canal overgrowth was also observed in mig-14/Wls mutants, while loss of mig-5/Dishevelled or dsh-1/Dishevelled resulted in a partially penetrant overgrowth phenotype (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: The loss of egl-20 and mig-1 partially rescued the canal overgrowth in lin-17.
source: Surprisingly, the loss of egl-20 and mig-1 also partially rescued the canal overgrowth in lin-17, even though neither of them displayed canal shortening on its own.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: mig-1 suppressed canal shortening in cfz-2.
source: In contrast, mig-1 suppressed canal shortening in cfz-2.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: The most prominent canal shortening was observed in cwn-1; cfz-2 or cwn-2; cfz-2 double mutants.
source: The most prominent canal shortening was observed in cwn-1; cfz-2 or cwn-2; cfz-2 double mutants (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 7B.

claim: Three instead of two posterior canal branches were detected in 11% of cwn-1; cfz-2 and 15% of cwn-2; cfz-2 double mutants.
source: Apart from shortening, three instead of two posterior canal branches were detected in 11% of cwn-1; cfz-2 and 15% of cwn-2; cfz-2 double mutants (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7C.

claim: At least two Wnt-dependent pathways are acting during the extension of the excretory canal.
source: These data suggest that at least two Wnt-dependent pathways are acting during the extension of the excretory canal, one involving lin-44, lin-17, dsh-1 and mig-5 that is responsible for determining the stopping point for the growing canal, and one involving cwn-1, cwn-2, and cfz-2 that contributes to the canal growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of Wnt and Frizzled mutants.

claim: One Wnt pathway involving lin-44, lin-17, dsh-1 and mig-5 is responsible for determining the stopping point for the growing canal.
source: These data suggest that at least two Wnt-dependent pathways are acting during the extension of the excretory canal, one involving lin-44, lin-17, dsh-1 and mig-5 that is responsible for determining the stopping point for the growing canal, and one involving cwn-1, cwn-2, and cfz-2 that contributes to the canal growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of Wnt and Frizzled mutants.

claim: One Wnt pathway involving cwn-1, cwn-2, and cfz-2 contributes to the canal growth.
source: These data suggest that at least two Wnt-dependent pathways are acting during the extension of the excretory canal, one involving lin-44, lin-17, dsh-1 and mig-5 that is responsible for determining the stopping point for the growing canal, and one involving cwn-1, cwn-2, and cfz-2 that contributes to the canal growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of Wnt and Frizzled mutants.

claim: No difference in canal length was detected between wild type controls and lin-17, lin-44, and mig-14 mutants within the 24 hr interval after hatching.

source: Phosphorylation of µ2 at Thr156 by AAK1 enhances the binding affinity of AP2 to the sorting signals of endocytosed proteins (Ricotta et al., 2002).
